lines.t: Eighty percent of this grade is three multiple-choice exams, in class, closed note. So the whole game is whether you can do something new with a definition under time pressure.

Which is exactly what Stromme says separates the A students. Memorisers do fine until a question asks them to apply a building block in a way they have not seen. The top grades go to people who learned the connections.
So this episode is the blocks. Ten chapters, the formula sheet, and the traps that cost the most points.
And a self-test at the end. But do the problem sets yourself — the connections come from doing problems, not from listening to me.
The grade, precisely.

Eighty percent exams, twenty percent problem sets, plus up to three percent extra credit from Top Hat. Your best exam counts thirty percent, the other two twenty-five each. Or you can swap Midterm Three for a comprehensive final worth forty percent if that helps you.
The dates.

Midterm One, September thirtieth, a Wednesday, in class. Midterm Two, November fourth. And Midterm Three or the final in the official exam slot — for the nine oh five section, Tuesday December fifteenth, three to five.
Two things in the syllabus quietly protect you.

Your lowest problem set is dropped, and missing ones can be emailed at the end of term for fifty percent. And about five classes of Top Hat are excused. But there are no problem set extensions. Ever, for any reason.
Now his four-step study method, because he actually tells you how to study.

Step one. Review each slide deck right after lecture, and be ruthless. Could you explain every point to a friend, out loud, with no notes? He says ninety-five percent of students fool themselves here.
That is the important one.

It is. I recognise this is not the same as I can explain this. Step two — do the problem sets alone first. Every assigned problem deliberately targets one building block, so ask yourself which concept it is testing. Then a friend, then a T A.
Step three.
Read the answer key carefully, including for questions you got right. A right answer for the wrong reason still costs you on the exam.
And step four.

Only then, practice exams. Timed, no notes. Then modify every question — what would make a different answer correct? Can you reverse it, Jeopardy style? Can you swap in a related concept? And he asks you to do that rewriting yourself rather than having a model generate practice questions for you.
Chapters one and two. Vocabulary, and cheap points on Midterm One.

Economics is the study of how agents choose to allocate scarce resources, and how those choices affect society. An economic agent is anyone making choices — a person, a household, a firm, a government.
Positive versus normative.

Positive is an objective description or prediction — falsifiable. A fifteen dollar minimum wage reduces teen employment by two percent. Normative is a value judgment about what should happen. The minimum wage should be fifteen dollars.
And the trap.
A positive statement can be wrong and still be positive. What makes it positive is that it could be checked against evidence — not that it is true. Falsifiable in principle, not true.
Now the three principles that frame the whole course.
Optimisation — agents choose whatever gives them the best value. Equilibrium — and memorise both halves of this one. And empiricism.
Give me the full definition of equilibrium.
Everyone is optimising, and nobody believes they would personally be better off changing their own choice, holding everyone else's choices fixed. Students drop that second half constantly.
And empiricism.

Economics mostly cannot run petri-dish experiments, for ethical and practical reasons. So it answers cause-and-effect questions two ways. Theory-driven — build a model, change one thing, see what happens. And statistics-driven — find clever ways to imitate a controlled experiment using observational data. Real research sits on a spectrum between them.
Chapter three. The single most reused idea in the course.

Opportunity cost is the value of the best foregone alternative. Note best, singular — not the sum of everything you gave up. You use it two ways: as a broad idea, always asking what you are giving up, and to put a dollar value on time.
Sunk cost.
Money or time already spent that you cannot get back. Ignore it completely when deciding what to do next. It is identical under every option, so it cannot change which option is best.
Now the two routes to the same answer.

Net benefit is total benefit minus total cost, and the optimum is where net benefit is highest. Total analysis computes net benefit for every option and picks the biggest. Marginal analysis looks at one extra unit at a time — keep going while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost, and stop where they cross.
Work his example.

How many hours to study, where each hour costs you twenty dollars of foregone work. One hour: sixty dollars of benefit, twenty of cost, net forty. Two hours: net sixty. Three hours: net sixty-five. Four hours: net fifty-five.
So total analysis says?

Three hours, at sixty-five dollars. And marginal analysis agrees — hour three is worth twenty-five against a cost of twenty, so take it. Hour four is worth ten against twenty, so stop. Same answer, less arithmetic. That is why marginal analysis wins.
And the exam trap.
Marginal benefit falls as you do more of something, and marginal cost usually rises. The optimum is where they cross — not where total benefit is highest, and not where cost is lowest.
Chapter four. The workhorse. Expect the most exam questions here.

Start with what the heights of the curves mean, because that is what makes the crossing point efficient rather than just tidy. Demand height is willingness to pay — the buyer's marginal benefit. Supply height is willingness to accept — the seller's marginal cost.
And equilibrium.

Where the curves cross. Above the equilibrium price, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded — excess supply, so sellers cut price. Below it, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied — excess demand, so buyers bid the price up.
Now the number one tested thing in the course.

Movement along versus shift of a curve. A change in the good's own price moves you along the curve. A change in anything else shifts the whole curve. And here is the rule to hold onto: if the price changed on its own, do not shift the curve.
What shifts demand?

Income — normal versus inferior goods. The price of substitutes, used instead of each other, like Coke and Pepsi. The price of complements, used together, like printers and ink. Tastes. Expectations. And the number of buyers.
And supply?
Input prices. Technology. Expectations. And the number of sellers.
What if both curves shift?
There is a shortcut. Whichever effect — price or quantity — the two shifts push in the same direction is certain. The other one is ambiguous, and depends on which shift is bigger.
Price ceilings and floors.

An effective price ceiling sits below equilibrium — rent control. At that low price buyers want a lot and sellers offer little, so there is excess demand, a shortage. And trade only happens up to the quantity supplied, because sellers will not supply more.
And a floor.
Sits above equilibrium — the minimum wage — and gives the mirror image: excess supply, with trade only up to the quantity demanded.
Watch the wording, though.

Ceiling gives excess demand. Floor gives excess supply. If the answer choices say shortage and surplus, map them from excess demand and excess supply rather than trying to recall the label — that is exactly where students flip the answer. And a ceiling above equilibrium, or a floor below it, does nothing at all. It is not binding.
Chapter five. The most calculation-heavy topic on the first two midterms.
Consumer surplus first. It is what you were willing to pay minus what you actually paid, summed over all the units you bought.
Two ways to find it.

From a table, subtract the price from each unit's willingness to pay and add up the positive ones. From a graph, it is the area below the demand curve and above the price, out to the quantity traded — usually a triangle, so one half base times height.
Now elasticity. Give me the formula the course uses.

The midpoint, or arc, formula. Elasticity equals the change in quantity divided by the average of the two quantities, all divided by the change in price divided by the average of the two prices. That is the only elasticity formula you need.
Work the example.

Price rises from four dollars to six, quantity falls from a hundred to eighty. The percentage change in quantity is minus twenty over ninety, which is minus twenty-two point two percent. The percentage change in price is two over five, forty percent. Divide: minus zero point five six. Absolute value below one, so inelastic.
And what happens to revenue?

Elastic, absolute value above one — quantity reacts a lot, so a price rise makes revenue fall. Unit elastic, equal to one — revenue unchanged, and at its maximum. Inelastic, below one — a price rise makes revenue rise.
Give me the one-line rule.
Revenue moves in the direction of price when demand is inelastic, and against it when demand is elastic.
Now the conceptual trap.

Elasticity is not slope. A straight-line demand curve has one constant slope and a changing elasticity — elastic on the upper half, unit elastic exactly at the midpoint, inelastic on the lower half. And total revenue is largest at that midpoint.
What makes demand more elastic?
More close substitutes. The good being a luxury rather than a necessity. A large share of your budget. A long time to adjust. And a narrowly defined market — Honda Civics is more elastic than cars.
The other two elasticities.

Cross-price elasticity — the sign tells you the relationship. Positive means substitutes, negative means complements. Income elasticity — positive means a normal good, negative means an inferior good.
And the bang-for-your-buck condition.

You are optimising when marginal benefit per dollar is equal across goods — marginal benefit of X over price of X equals marginal benefit of Y over price of Y. If one side is bigger, buy more of that good.
Chapter six. Lots of formulas, but they are all just definitions.
Vocabulary first. Short run means at least one input is fixed. Long run means everything is variable, including whether to exist at all.
Why does marginal cost eventually rise?
The law of diminishing returns. Adding more of one input to fixed inputs eventually raises output by smaller and smaller amounts. Ten cooks, one oven.
Economic versus accounting profit.

Economic profit subtracts all opportunity costs, including the salary you gave up. Accounting profit subtracts only explicit money costs. So economic profit is always less than or equal to accounting profit.
Now the picture. Why does marginal cost cut the averages at their minimums?
Because an average falls while the next value is below it, and rises once the next value is above it. So the curves cross exactly at the bottom. That is not a coincidence, it is arithmetic.
And the gap between average total cost and average variable cost?
That is average fixed cost, and it shrinks forever as fixed cost spreads over more units.
How much to produce, and whether to produce at all.

Produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Under perfect competition price equals marginal revenue, so produce where price equals marginal cost. Then compare price to average total cost at that quantity for profit or loss, and the size of it is quantity times the gap.
Shutdown versus exit.

Short run, shut down if price is below minimum average variable cost — above that you are at least covering variable costs and chipping away at fixed costs, which are sunk in the short run. Long run, exit if price is below minimum average total cost, because nothing is fixed anymore. And breakeven price is minimum average total cost, where economic profit is exactly zero.
The firm's supply curve.

Its marginal cost curve above the relevant shutdown point. Add firms horizontally for market supply. And in the long run, positive profits attract entry, which shifts market supply right and pushes price down — until price equals minimum long-run average total cost and economic profit is zero.
And the trap he warns about directly.

When computing marginals from a table, divide by the change in quantity. Do not just subtract one row from the next. If output jumps from ten to fourteen units, marginal cost is the change in total cost divided by four — not the change in total cost.
Supply elasticity.

Ask one question: does this make the producer more flexible? Holding inventories, non-perishable goods, the long run, easily adjusted variable inputs — all more elastic. Heavy reliance on fixed inputs — less elastic.
Chapter seven. And he says to favour the slides over the textbook here.

Total surplus is consumer surplus plus producer surplus — the whole triangle between the two curves, left of the efficient quantity. Every unit left of it has marginal benefit above marginal cost, so it is worth trading. Every unit right of it costs more to make than it is worth.
So efficient means?
Total surplus is maximised. That is all it means. A perfectly competitive market lands exactly there.
Deadweight loss.
The surplus destroyed when a market does not trade the efficient quantity. On a graph it is the triangle between demand and supply over the units that failed to trade — one half base times height.
Pareto efficient versus Pareto improvement.
Pareto efficient means you cannot make anyone better off without making someone else worse off. A Pareto improvement is a change that makes at least one person better off and nobody worse off.
And the equity-efficiency tradeoff.
Efficiency is the size of total surplus. Equity is who gets it. The biggest pie is not necessarily fairly sliced, and economics alone cannot tell you the right balance — that is a normative question.
Chapter nine. Externalities. And chapter eight is skipped.
An externality is a spillover — a cost or benefit landing on someone who was not part of the transaction. The market ignores it, so the market gets the quantity wrong.
Name the four curves.

Marginal private benefit — the value to the buyer, and this is the demand curve. Marginal social benefit — that plus benefits spilling onto everyone else. Marginal private cost — the cost to the seller, and this is the supply curve. Marginal social cost — that plus costs spilling onto everyone else.
Where does the market trade, and where should it?

Private parties trade where marginal private benefit equals marginal private cost. Society's optimum is where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost. When those differ, the gap is deadweight loss.
Negative externality — which way does the market err?

Overproduction. Marginal social cost sits above marginal private cost, so the market quantity exceeds the optimal quantity. Flip it for a positive externality like vaccines or education — marginal social benefit sits above marginal private benefit, and the market underproduces.
The Coase theorem.

If property rights are clearly assigned and transaction costs are low, the parties can bargain their way to the efficient quantity on their own — no matter who initially holds the right. Who holds the right changes who pays whom. It does not change the efficient quantity.
And when does it fail?
Too many parties, murky rights, or expensive bargaining. Which is exactly why it does not solve climate change.
Government fixes.

Command-and-control sets direct rules — caps, bans, mandated technology. Market-based tools — taxes, subsidies, tradable permits — change prices so private incentives line up with social ones, and then let firms decide how to respond.
Chapter twelve. Monopoly.

Market power is the ability to set price above marginal cost. It is a spectrum, not a switch — perfect competition at one end with zero power, pure monopoly at the other. Two things move a firm along it: how unique its good is, and how strong the barriers to entry are.
Two kinds of barrier.
Legal — patents, licences, government-granted franchises. And natural — huge economies of scale, control of a key resource, network effects.
Why does marginal revenue lie below demand?

A monopolist is the market, so to sell one more unit it must lower the price — and not just on that unit, on every unit. So marginal revenue is the price of the new unit minus the revenue lost on all the previous ones. For a straight-line demand curve, marginal revenue has the same intercept and twice the slope.
The two-step move.
Find the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Then go straight up to the demand curve to read the price.
And the classic mistake.
Setting the price where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. That intersection gives you the quantity only. Price always comes off the demand curve — it is what buyers will pay for that quantity.
Perfect price discrimination. This is the striking one.

Charging every buyer exactly their willingness to pay. The result: the firm produces the efficient quantity, so deadweight loss is zero and the outcome is efficient. But consumer surplus is also zero, and the firm captures the entire surplus.
Efficient and not fair.
The cleanest proof in the course that efficiency is not the same as fairness. And a great question for testing whether you actually understand that.
Chapter thirteen. Game theory.
Every game has three ingredients: players, strategies and payoffs. You cover two types — simultaneous-move games with a payoff matrix, and extensive-form games with a tree.
Nash equilibrium versus dominant strategy.

A Nash equilibrium is a pair of strategies where both players are playing a best response, so neither would want to unilaterally switch. Notice that is just the course definition of equilibrium applied to games. A dominant strategy is your best response no matter what the other player does.
How do you solve a matrix?

Take player one's payoffs and, for each of player two's columns, mark player one's best. Then take player two's payoffs and, for each of player one's rows, mark player two's best. Any cell marked twice is a Nash equilibrium.
The prisoner's dilemma, with the numbers.

Quiet-Quiet pays two, two. Fink-Fink pays one, one. And the off-diagonals pay three to the finker and zero to the quiet one. If player two plays Quiet, player one gets three from Fink against two from Quiet — so Fink. If player two plays Fink, player one gets one from Fink against zero — so Fink again.
So Fink is dominant.

For both players. Fink-Fink is the unique Nash equilibrium at one, one — even though both would be better off at two, two. That gap between individual rationality and the group outcome is the entire point of the dilemma.
And game trees.

Solve by backward induction. Start at the end, work out what the last player does at each node, cross off the branches they would never take, then work backwards knowing how they will respond. That is how you see that a threat to fight is not credible, because carrying it out would hurt the threatener.
Closing topics. Chapters fourteen and sixteen, but only the slide-level ideas.

Results along the market-power spectrum interpolate. A market between competition and monopoly gets an outcome between the two — some markup, some deadweight loss, but less of each than pure monopoly.
Collusion.

Rival firms cooperating to act like a monopolist and keep prices high. And notice it is a prisoner's dilemma — each firm's private incentive is to cheat and undercut, which is exactly why cartels are unstable.
How do you measure concentration?

Not by counting firms. The H H I — the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index — is the sum of each firm's market share squared, using percentages. Four firms at twenty-five percent each gives four times six hundred and twenty-five, so two thousand five hundred. One firm at a hundred percent gives ten thousand.
And why share rather than count?
Because twenty firms where one holds ninety-five percent is not a competitive market. The number of firms tells you very little.
Asymmetric information. Two problems, and the exam will want you to tell them apart.

Adverse selection hides a type, and it happens before the deal — only sick people buy the insurance. Moral hazard hides an action, and it happens after the deal — insured drivers drive more recklessly.
The death spiral.

Insurers raise premiums to cover a sick pool. The healthiest remaining people drop out. The pool gets sicker. Premiums rise again. Repeat until the market can collapse. That is adverse selection eating itself.
And the principal-agent distinction, which you said he would write a question around.

A principal-agent relationship is one party acting on behalf of another — employee and employer, contractor and homeowner, doctor and patient. And careful: not every principal-agent relationship has moral hazard. It only becomes moral hazard when the principal cannot observe what the agent actually does.
Formula sheet. Say them so I can hear them.

Costs. Total cost is total fixed cost plus total variable cost. Marginal cost is the change in total cost divided by the change in quantity. Average total cost is total cost over quantity. Average variable cost is total variable cost over quantity. Average fixed cost is total fixed cost over quantity.
Revenue and profit.
Total revenue is price times quantity. Profit is total revenue minus total cost, which also equals quantity times price minus average total cost.
Perfect competition.
Price equals marginal revenue equals average revenue. Produce where price equals marginal cost. And the long-run price is minimum average total cost.
Surplus.
Consumer surplus is under demand and above price. Producer surplus is above marginal cost and under price. Total surplus is the two together. And a triangle is one half base times height.
And the social optimum.
Marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost, against a market outcome at marginal private benefit equals marginal private cost.
Self-test. Twelve questions. Answer out loud before the answer comes.
One. A question says the price of coffee rose. Do you shift the demand curve?
No. A change in the good's own price is a movement along the curve. Only a change in something else — income, related prices, tastes, expectations, the number of buyers — shifts it.
Two. Price goes from four to six, quantity from a hundred to eighty. Elastic or inelastic, and what happens to revenue?

Percentage change in quantity is minus twenty-two point two. Percentage change in price is forty. Elasticity is minus zero point five six — inelastic. And revenue moves with price when demand is inelastic, so revenue rises.
Three. A table shows output jumping from ten to fourteen units. How do you compute marginal cost?
Change in total cost divided by four, not just the change in total cost. Always divide by the change in quantity. This is the trap he warns about directly.
Four. You found the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost for a monopolist. Where does the price come from?
Straight up to the demand curve at that quantity. Setting the price at the intersection itself is the classic mistake.
Five. Why is zero economic profit not a failure?

In long-run competition it means you are earning exactly what you could earn elsewhere — all opportunity costs are already subtracted. Economic profit is always less than or equal to accounting profit.
Six. Perfect price discrimination — efficient or fair?

Efficient and not fair. The firm produces the efficient quantity so deadweight loss is zero, but consumer surplus is zero and the firm captures the entire surplus. The cleanest proof that efficiency is not fairness.
Seven. An effective price ceiling — describe it.

It sits below equilibrium. Buyers want a lot, sellers offer little: excess demand, a shortage, with trade only up to the quantity supplied. A ceiling above equilibrium is not binding and does nothing.
Eight. Adverse selection or moral hazard: insured drivers drive more recklessly?
Moral hazard — a hidden action, after the deal. Adverse selection is a hidden type, before the deal: only sick people buy the insurance.
Nine. Does every principal-agent relationship have moral hazard?
No. Only when the principal cannot observe what the agent actually does. That is exactly the kind of distinction he writes a multiple-choice question around.
Ten. Four firms each hold twenty-five percent. What is the H H I, and why not just count firms?

Four times twenty-five squared — four times six hundred and twenty-five — is two thousand five hundred. A pure monopoly is ten thousand. It captures share, and twenty firms where one holds ninety-five percent is not a competitive market.
Eleven. How do you solve a game tree, and what does it reveal?

Backward induction. Start at the end, work out the last player's move at each node, cross off branches they would never take, and work backwards. It is how you see that a threat to fight is not credible, because carrying it out would hurt the threatener.
Twelve. A positive statement can be false. Is it still positive?
Yes. What makes a statement positive is that it could be checked against evidence. Falsifiable in principle, not true.
Last pass. The traps that cost the most points, rapid fire.
Shift versus movement. Own price changed, move along. Anything else, shift.
Next.
Sunk costs. Already spent, already gone. Never a reason to keep going.
Next.
Marginals from tables. Divide by the change in quantity.
Next.
Monopoly price. Quantity from marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Price from the demand curve above it.
Next.
Elasticity is not slope. A straight demand curve has one slope and many elasticities.
Next.
Economic versus accounting profit. Zero economic profit is normal and fine in long-run competition.
Next.
Efficient is not fair. Perfect price discrimination is the counterexample.
Next.
Positive versus normative. Falsifiable in principle, not true.
Next.
Ceiling versus floor. Ceiling is below equilibrium, excess demand. Floor is above, excess supply. Draw the horizontal line before you answer.
And the last one.
Adverse selection versus moral hazard. Type before the deal, action after it.
That is the building blocks. Now go do what he actually asked in step four.
Work the practice exams cold, and rewrite every question until you can see what it is really testing. That is the part that moves a B to an A.
